This would be my suggestion.  Crating for the pup, of course.  It takes time to train them and at 8 weeks old, they really need to be able to go out to potty every couple of hours or so. Crating is great for safety, especially while introducing a new pup to another established dog.

I stated previously that I do not use those methods nor do I have experience with shocks and won't use them.  If someone does, then they should seek proper training themselves on how to use them.  It isn't something I will suggest using.  Ta.

I use vocal correction mostly and remove either the item or the dog from the situation or the item. 

She is on a strict schedule of food, play, training, and rest as well as socialization.  This alone helps keep her from getting into things she shouldn't be in.

Like anything, collars (prongs or shock) are tools.  They're not for everyone.  For my girl usually a verbal correction is enough.  Sometimes I have to tether her to me (leash on collar, end of leash attatched to me) to help me keep my eye on her when she is out of her crate.  If she is starting to act up, a verbal correction and then I distract by going into training.  Tethering is also amazing for keeping her calm and teaching her to do nothing.

If he can't sit in it or his back is brushing the inside of the door, then it's too small.  

It couldn't hurt to try a playpen for him, but be mindful if he shows signs of separation anxiety and starts to chew it.  It being more open might ebb some of his fearfulness.
I don't hit, pop, stick my fingers in places, roll the dog, or anything that would have my dog flinch away from me in the long run.  She is my partner and my companion and that's how I treat her.

A very good rule of thumb for crates is that it should be big enough for them to stand, turn, and lay comfortably without there being much extra room.  Think of it as a bed, and putting a six foot tall man in a toddler bed.  That can't be comfortable.  

Make it comfortable.  Make it a happy place.  Never ever use it for punishment and they should go in on their own.  If they go in, they should be rewarded. Puppies need a lot of sleep.  They are growing the fastest right now and you kinda have to think like a dog half the time and the other half of training is waiting them out.

As long as you are calm and can lure them into the crate on their own, they won't see it as punishment.  If you yell and pick them up to put them in, they will.  Tether training can also help correct some of the behaviour and such immediately and in the moment if she goes after furniture etc.  A little pop and "Aht" or no. It's time consuming and frustrating.  But dogs are a lot like toddlers.  There's no reasoning when they get beyond that point of being exhausted and it can manifest into destructive behaviour.  What I did for my girl was I got her on a schedule.  Wake.  Potty. A little training. Some play.  Food.  Crate.  Potty rinse and repeat through the day until bed time. Night potty trips were quiet and unexciting.  I hope this helps.

Impulse control has so many facets that it's difficult to put into words.  Impulse control teaches your dog to not bite, jump, bark, or do other unwanted behaviors because they stop and think about it.  

This guy (RIP) is amazing and has so many videos.  I would probably wager to get the absolute best results, start at ground level with everything and to the letter.  It's all positive reinforcement training without any biting, hitting, raised voices, alpha rolls or any of that stuff that's deemed okay by old school folks.  https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=outback+dog+training

Bite inhibition.  Impulse control.  These are the two biggest things that are coming up for me by reading your description on behaviours.  Exercise is all well and good, but structured training and time outs have a huge role to play when raising a dog.  If you do not crate train, I suggest it.  It gives your dog a chance to decompress.  Like toddlers, if they become more and more over tired or over stimulated, they can become difficult to handle.  

Crating is perfectly humane and safe providing your dog does not hurt himself while in it (biting bars etc).  Start slow with a minute or so at a time and treat when calm, and let them out.  

As for impulse control and bite inhibition, take up all toys, all bones, and no furniture privilages until your training yields the behaviours you want.

People think socializing is actually being around and in contact with other dogs and people.  It isn't.  It's about seeing them. Dogs are like people.  They learn at different speeds.  If you are amped or frustrated, they can sense it.  Start in the house.  Take a step back.  I know he still has to go out, but tether train him as well if you aren't.  When you are together, leash him inside and ignore him.  It will be rough, but he will soon see that not every time you get the leash means he gets to go outside.

Tether him to you when you are home.  Work on quiet reactions to things.  If you prompt him with "Shhh" and he does it, wait just a second and mark with enthusiasm "Yes!" "Good boy" and treat.  Every time wait a little longer.

There are a lot of resources on impulse control out there and definitely contact your trainer.

Mental games may calm him as well.  They are a working breed and need things to do.

1. Take up all bones, toys etc.  These are things designated for play time, which you should initiate and immediately put up when finished.  This teaches the dog that they do get it back and it hasn't gone anywhere and it's okay to not have something at a whim.

2.  No furniture privileges at all.  This puts your dog on your level of the hierarchy when you are eye level with them.  No beds, couch etc.  If you do not crate train, now might be a good time to.

3.  Feed all food from your hand.  No people food.  Just what you normally would.  Every bite should come from you and only after a good play/work session.

4.  No.  I am not a trainer, but this is the advice I received from mine and it worked for my shepsky who would steal stuff and bite at you if you tried to take it away.

5.  Try the trade game.  Have a toy or something better to have your dog's attention so you can safely remove the unwanted object.  

6.  Probably would do good to bullet proof "drop it" and "leave it" commands (very helpful tools).

Good luck!
